articles.title_zh: Musk makes $18 billion SpaceX stock pledge for every kid in America
articles.content_orig:
Former Deputy Treasury Secretary Michael Faulkender analyzes the potential expansion of Trump accounts for adults. He also weighs in on the challenges China's domestic economy is facing.
SpaceX announced Wednesday that it will contribute one share of its stock to every currently active Trump Account, with CEO Elon Musk pledging to personally match the company's donation.
The aerospace company's commitment follows Musk's pledge earlier this year to give every child in America a share of the company.
Musk elaborated on the planned stock giveaway in a post on X Wednesday evening, saying every child in America would receive an additional share from him personally.
"Every child in America will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from me personally," Musk wrote.
TRUMP ACCOUNTS HIT MAJOR MILESTONE AS FAMILY CONTRIBUTIONS SURPASS $1 BILLION
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pledged to personally match the company's planned donation of one share of stock to every currently active Trump Account. (Getty Images)
SpaceX said the planned contribution, which could be worth billions of dollars, would give the next generation of Americans a stake in the company's future.
"SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit."
SpaceX, whose shares were trading just above $127 Wednesday, said it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account.
SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell also announced a separate personal donation of more than 2 million shares of the company's stock.
Musk pledged last month to give every child in America a share of SpaceX in 2027, although he did not provide details at the time about how the proposed giveaway would work.
"Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk wrote on X in October.
SpaceX confirmed Wednesday that his latest commitment is part of that pledge.
‘DATA CENTERS IN SPACE’: FCC CLEARS SPACEX FOR 1M SATELLITES TO ‘EXTEND AMERICA’S LEAD IN SUPERINTELLIGENCE’
SpaceX announced Wednesday that it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account. (Alisha Jucevic/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The announcement comes just one day after the Treasury Department revealed that contributions from friends and family members to Trump Accounts had surpassed $1 billion.
With the holiday season approaching, the pledged contributions represent another boost for the program, which provides tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children under 18 with valid Social Security numbers.
More than 3 million friends and family members have contributed to individual accounts, with total deposits exceeding $9 billion when philanthropic gifts and federal seed contributions are included, according to a Treasury Department statement provided to FOX Business.
Children born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, are eligible for a one-time $1,000 seed contribution from the federal government.
While Trump Accounts have been created for eligible children under 18, parents and guardians must claim the accounts before they can manage them or enable contributions.
GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO BY CLICKING HERE
Trump Accounts are set to receive additional contributions from SpaceX and Elon Musk after total deposits in the children's investment program surpassed $9 billion. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)
The Treasury Department announced last month that approximately 70 million Trump Accounts had been established for eligible children, although it was not immediately clear how many had been activated.
FOX Business reached out to SpaceX for comment.

articles.title_orig: Angry young men turn against their elders in ‘two Spains’ election
articles.title_zh: Angry young men turn against their elders in ‘two Spains’ election
articles.content_orig:
After eight years of Socialist-led government under Pedro Sánchez, Spain is at a crossroads.
Snap elections are taking place on Sunday 29 November, and voters face a choice of continued left-wing rule or a conservative-led government, with the likely support of far-right Vox.
Sánchez called this vote eight months early after MPs rejected planned changes to Spain's housing laws.
He was responding to nationwide protests after an 87-year-old woman called Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her rented flat in Madrid and later died.
But his government lost the support of a centre-right party called Junts from the north-eastern region of Catalonia which sought to protect the rights of property owners.
Housing remains one of the hot-button issues for voters, but they are also focused on the high cost of living, corruption and immigration. And the election takes place within weeks of a devastating rail disaster that has shattered confidence in Spain’s high-speed rail network.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo's conservative People's Party is narrowly ahead of the Socialist PSOE in most polls.
He has spoken of Spain being probably at "the most significant moment in our country for the past 50 years", and he aims to "repair the state, regenerate democracy, reunited the nation and recover Spain's ambition and self-esteem". But it is unlikely he could do anything without the backing of Vox, who are third in the opinion polls.
For more on Feijóo, Sánchez and who else to watch in this election - read here .
Spain has a population of almost 50 million, and almost 39 million people have the right to vote for the Congress and the upper house, the Senate. The polls open at 09:00 (08:00 GMT) on Sunday and close at 20:00 (19:00 GMT). Provisional results will start appearing an hour later.
Spain's property prices and rents have soared by more than 80% from 2015 to 2025, and wages have not kept pace.
Spain has a combination of high demand and scarce supply: the Bank of Spain estimates 700,000 homes are needed to ease the pressure.
The result is that millions of Spaniards have little chance to buy a house, while they live in fear of eviction if their rent is increased. On 11 November, four million Spaniards were galvanised into joining the first general strike since 2012, according to the unions.
Pedro Sánchez has embraced housing reform as a big campaign issue and left-wing parties have promised rent controls and protection against eviction, while the right is focusing on building more homes, tax breaks for homebuyers and planning deregulation.
Support for the Socialists is down from 2023, but even then he came second in the race and relied on the backing of other parties, mainly on the left, to stay in power.
Securing a majority requires 176 seats out of the 350 in Spain's Congress. This time the other left-wing parties whose support he needs, in particular the Broad Front (Frente Amplio), have fallen back and the big questions now are more about Feijóo's conservatives.
"It is a demobilisation of the left. Sánchez's party is not doing well," says Jacobo Ramos Folch, Policy Analyst and visiting professor at the University of Navarra.
"That lack of majority is really a reality – and the rise of Vox. What is changing that shift of majorities is the rise of Vox."
Vox have been around since 2013 but polls suggest this time they could almost double their 33 seats in Spain's lower house, the Congress.
Their big themes are "national priority" – putting Spanish citizens first for subsidies and welfare, along with repatriating migrants "in an illegal situation" and "remigration" of foreigners who do not contribute to Spain.
Migration has become a key challenge for Spain, and Alberto Nuñez Feijóo has accused his rival of being a "problem for Europe when it comes to immigration" after the influx of tens of thousands of migrants into the exclave of Ceuta from neighbouring Morocco in July.
This month too, the Canary Island of El Hierro has seen record arrivals, with 2,000 people landing there on 24 November. Abascal has spoken of "another invasion".
And yet a recent CIS survey put it far behind housing, cost of living, healthcare and working conditions.
The PP and Vox have bitterly criticised the Socialist-led government for a drive to legalise unauthorised migrants this year that attracted 1.2 million applications.
Feijóo's party wants to see more controlled immigration. Vox has called for mass deportations.
Feijóo has accused the Socialists of being "the most corrupt party" that Spain has ever seen, and a number of cases have involved Sánchez's inner circle and family.
People should distinguish between real and "fictitious" corruption allegations, says Sánchez.
His former transport minister José Luis Ábalos has been given 24 years in prison over multiple corruption offences.
Leading party figure Santos Cerdán awaits trial for alleged bribery and denies wrongdoing.
Sánchez's wife Begoña Gómez faces trial for alleged misuse of public funds and using her marriage to further her academic career. She denies wrongdoing. And his brother David Sánchez has been banned from public office for nine years for administrative misconduct.
Feijóo has made clear his objective is to form a majority and make "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox. As far as a coalition is concerned, he says he will respect the will of Spanish voters, but maintains Abascal has never talked to him about running any ministries.
The PP leader is clear that Vox's national priority policy would run counter to Spain's constitution and European Union treaties: "No-one can sign illegal agreements."
Even if they were to go into coalition, Camino Mortera-Martinez of the Centre for European Reform, and a former European affairs adviser to the Spanish prime minister is not convinced Vox would wield much influence.
"They're not going to get any of the core ministries. They're not going to get defence or home affairs or foreign policy or economy," she told the BBC. Even if they take over the education ministry, Mortera-Martinez argues education policy is largely devolved to Spain's regional governments.
Since 2022, Vox has worked with the PP in a series of regional coalition governments, holding ministries such as culture and tourism. At the time Feijóo had reservations about Vox joining the conservatives in government in Castilla y León.
The following year they went into coalition with the conservatives in Valencia, Aragón, Murcia, and Extremadura, but pulled out of all five governments in 2024 when they refused to accept unaccompanied migrant children being moved to their regions.
They have since signed new coalition pacts with the PP in Extremadura, Aragón, Castilla y León and Andalusia.
Unlike many European countries Spain has 17 autonomous communities (and two cities) that have their own parliament and their own powers. Catalonia in the north-east and the Basque Country in the north have their own police forces.
The regions matter to Sunday's result. Catalonia alone has 48 seats out of the 350 in Spain's parliament, and the Socialists have recently come to rely on regional parties for support.
Sánchez's government relied on the support of Basque separatists Bildu and two Catalan parties, ERC on the left and Junts on the right. But when Junts refused to back his housing reform, he decided to dissolve parliament.
Spain is made up of 50 constituencies which each have a minimum of two seats.
The exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla both have one, and the other 248 seats are divided proportionally according to voter numbers.
Madrid province will have 38 seats, Barcelona 32 and Valencia 16.
To win a seat, a party has to win 3% of the vote in a province, but in smaller provinces with fewer seats parties generally need more than that.

articles.title_orig: At least 31 killed in Egypt vehicle fire, Health Ministry says
articles.title_zh: At least 31 killed in Egypt vehicle fire, Health Ministry says
articles.content_orig:
At least 31 people were ⁠⁠killed, and ⁠⁠another 21 were injured when a vehicle carrying ‌‌petroleum products overturned and caught fire on a major ring ⁠⁠⁠⁠road in the Egyptian capital, Cairo, the ⁠Ministry of Health said on Wednesday.
The fire broke out above a tunnel in the al-Warak neighbourhood of Giza’s Imbabah district. The ring road connects key highways across Greater Cairo, linking the governorates of Cairo, ‌‌Giza and Qalyubia.
Local media reported that a truck swerved and hit the central reservation as it overturned, triggering an explosion. The fire has since been extinguished, according to local media.
Egypt’s public prosecutor announced an investigation into the crash and ordered the collection of DNA samples from the victims’ bodies. The judicial office also said 27 vehicles were burned.
The Health Ministry said 39 ambulances were sent to the site of the incident and that the injured were transferred to nearby hospitals.
Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said he would head to the crash scene himself.
The official spokesman for the Egyptian presidency said President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi “expresses his sincere condolences and sincere sympathy to the families of the victims” and wished them a speedy recovery.
According to an Egyptian Cabinet statement, Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly offered his condolences to the victims’ families and ordered that their medical expenses be covered by the state.
“The Ministry of Health and Population continues to closely monitor the situation and coordinate with the relevant authorities to ensure that the necessary medical care is provided to the injured,” a ministry statement read.

Musk later elaborated on the planned stock giveaway in a post on X Wednesday evening, saying every child in America would receive an additional share from him personally.
"Every child in America will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from me personally," Musk wrote.
TRUMP ACCOUNTS HIT MAJOR MILESTONE AS FAMILY CONTRIBUTIONS SURPASS $1 BILLION
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pledged to personally match the company's planned donation of one share of stock to every currently active Trump Account. (Getty Images / Getty Images)
SpaceX said the planned contribution, which could be worth billions of dollars, would give the next generation of Americans a stake in the company's future.
"SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit."
SpaceX, whose shares were trading just above $127 Wednesday, said it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account.
SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell also announced a separate personal donation of more than 2 million shares of the company's stock.
Musk pledged last month to give every child in America a share of SpaceX in 2027, although he did not provide details at the time about how the proposed giveaway would work.
"Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk wrote on X in October.
SpaceX confirmed Wednesday that his latest commitment is part of that pledge.
‘DATA CENTERS IN SPACE’: FCC CLEARS SPACEX FOR 1M SATELLITES TO ‘EXTEND AMERICA’S LEAD IN SUPERINTELLIGENCE’
SpaceX announced Wednesday that it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account. (Alisha Jucevic/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
The announcement comes just one day after the Treasury Department revealed that contributions from friends and family members to Trump Accounts had surpassed $1 billion.
With the holiday season approaching, the pledged contributions represent another boost for the program, which provides tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children under 18 with valid Social Security numbers.
More than 3 million friends and family members have contributed to individual accounts, with total deposits exceeding $9 billion when philanthropic gifts and federal seed contributions are included, according to a Treasury Department statement provided to FOX Business.
Children born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, are eligible for a one-time $1,000 seed contribution from the federal government.
While Trump Accounts have been created for eligible children under 18, parents and guardians must claim the accounts before they can manage them or enable contributions.

Trump Accounts are set to receive additional contributions from SpaceX and Elon Musk after total deposits in the children's investment program surpassed $9 billion. (Mandel NGAN / AFP / Getty Images)
The Treasury Department announced last month that approximately 70 million Trump Accounts had been established for eligible children, although it was not immediately clear how many had been activated.
Fox Business reached out to SpaceX for comment.

articles.title_orig: Who pays the new EU taxes? A breakdown of who will foot the bill
articles.title_zh: Who pays the new EU taxes? A breakdown of who will foot the bill
articles.content_orig:
EU leaders are engaged in intense discussion over the bloc's new seven-year budget before the end of the year, with member states butting heads over the overall size, spending priorities and how to finance it.
In terms of new resources Brussels intends to tap into, European Council President Antonio Costa proposed an ambitious mix of EU-wide taxes meant to generate about €60bn in revenue each year.
But who pays the bill? With Costa's compromise, the European Commission circulated an updated estimate of how much each Europe-wide tax is meant to generate, and which countries will bear most of the costs.
Between 2028 and 2034, Germany would be by far the country paying the highest share of EU taxes, with over €13bn in current prices, followed by Italy with €8bn. Despite being the bloc's second-largest economy, France merely ranks third, which explains Paris' strong support for new own resources.
However, the asymmetrical contribution to own resources is best understood in terms of what they would otherwise pay in national contributions based on their Gross National Income (GNI).
Costa's proposal made several adjustments to the EU taxes, mostly to accommodate objections from member states from central and eastern Europe, leaving southern European countries to pay the highest share.
On average, the tax of €2.25 per kilogram of uncollected electronic waste is by far the one expected to yield more revenues, with over €20bn expected per year, despite it being relatively less controversial than the Emissions Trading System (ETS), the Tobacco Tax or the digital levy.
While the e-waste contribution is the largest for most member states, how much each own resource will weigh on the national governments varies considerably, shaping the positioning of the member states.
The revenues expected from each tax are not fixed due to a number of reasons, including the fact that several of them will be adjusted for inflation.
The Commission projects the yields might significantly increase over time, with the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a tax on imports of carbon-intensive products, expected to more than double its revenues by 2034.
For the tax of €1.25 per kilogram of non-recycled plastic packaging waste, over half of the revenues are expected to come from the EU's four largest member states, France, Germany, Italy and Spain.
Similarly, the four EU countries would also account for over 60% of the revenues coming from an EU-wide digital services tax. France, Italy and Spain already have a digital levy at the national level, meaning they would lose these revenues in favour of Brussels.
The yields of the tobacco excise duty are also highly geographically concentrated, but in this case there is a less linear relation with the member states' population and reflects more national consumption habits and national excise duty levels.
Luxembourg, for instance, would make a significant contribution despite its relatively tiny size, as it sells large volumes of cigarettes and related products to consumers from neighbouring countries thanks to its lower prices.
For the tax on e-waste, which envisages a contribution from member states based on the share of electronic devices produced on their territory that are recycled, over 60% of the revenues would come from Germany, Italy and France, the EU's manufacturing powerhouses. By contrast, the Commission estimates Bulgaria would have to pay zero.
Giving 30% of the revenues generated from the Emissions Trading System (ETS), a carbon market for CO2-intensive industries, would be particularly advantageous for France, which would be in fourth position in terms of contribution, whilst it would penalise countries like Poland and Bulgaria compared to their economic size.
Italy would be the first payer for the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), with Belgium and Poland also punching above their weight in terms of contributions.

The People's Party of Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o is narrowly ahead in most opinion polls
After eight years of Socialist-led government under Pedro SÃ¡nchez, Spain is at a crossroads.
Snap elections are taking place on Sunday 29 November, and voters face a choice of continued left-wing rule or a conservative-led government, with the likely support of far-right Vox.
Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o's conservative People's Party is narrowly ahead of the Socialist PSOE in most polls.
He has spoken of Spain being probably at "the most significant moment in our country for the past 50 years", and he aims to "repair the state, regenerate democracy, reunited the nation and recover Spain's ambition and self-esteem". But it is unlikely he could do anything without the backing of Vox, who are third in the opinion polls.
For more on FeijÃ³o and who else to watch in this election - read here .
Spain has a population of almost 50 million, and almost 39 million people have the right to vote for the Congress and the upper house, the Senate. The polls open at 09:00 (08:00 GMT) on Sunday and close at 20:00 (19:00 GMT), when the first exit polls come out.
SÃ¡nchez called this vote eight months early after MPs rejected planned changes to Spain's housing laws.
He was responding to nationwide protests after an 87-year-old woman called Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her rented flat in Madrid and later died.
But his government lost the support of a centre-right party called Junts from the north-eastern region of Catalonia which sought to protect the rights of property owners.
Housing remains one of the hot-button issues for voters, but they are also focused on the high cost of living, corruption and immigration.
Spain saw its first general strike for 14 years this month over a shortage of housing and high rental costs
Spain's property prices and rents have soared by more than 80% from 2015 to 2025, and wages have not kept pace.
Spain has a combination of high demand and scarce supply: the Bank of Spain estimates 700,000 homes are needed to ease the pressure.
The result is that millions of Spaniards have little chance to buy a house, while they live in fear of eviction if their rent is increased. On 11 November, four million Spaniards were galvanised into joining the first general strike since 2012, according to the unions.
Pedro SÃ¡nchez has embraced housing reform as a big campaign issue and left-wing parties have promised rent controls and protection against eviction, while the right is focusing on building more homes, tax breaks for homebuyers and planning deregulation.
SÃ¡nchez's wife BegoÃ±a GÃ³mez has played an important role in the election campaign
Support for the Socialists is down from 2023, but even then he came second in the race and relied on the backing of other parties, mainly on the left, to stay in power. This time those other left-wing parties, in particular the Broad Front (Frente Amplio) have fallen back and the big questions now are more about FeijÃ³o's conservatives.
"It is a demobilisation of the left. Sanchez's party is not doing well," says Jacobo Ramos Folch, Policy Analyst and visiting professor at the University of Navarra.
"That lack of majority is really a reality â and the rise of Vox. What is changing that shift of majorities is the rise of Vox."
Vox have been around since 2013 but polls suggest this time they could almost double their 33 seats in Spain's lower house, the Congress.
Their big themes are "national priority" â putting Spanish citizens first for subsidies and welfare, along with repatriating migrants "in an illegal situation" and "remigration" of foreigners who do not contribute to Spain.
Pedro SÃ¡nchez (left), Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o (centre) and Santiago Abascal (right)
Migration has become a key challenge for Spain, and Alberto NuÃ±ez Feijoo has accused his rival of being a "problem for Europe when it comes to immigration" after the influx of tens of thousands of migrants into the exclave of Ceuta from neighbouring Morocco in July.
This month too, the Canary Island of El Hierro has seen record arrivals, with 2,000 people landing there on 24 November. Abascal has spoken of "another invasion".
And yet a recent CIS survey put it far behind housing, cost of living, healthcare and working conditions.
The PP and Vox have bitterly criticised the Socialist-led government for a drive to legalise unauthorised migrants this year that attracted 1.2 million applications.
FeijÃ³o's party wants to see more controlled immigration. Vox has called for mass deportations.
Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election
FeijÃ³o has accused the Socialists of being "the most corrupt party" that Spain had ever seen, and a number of cases have involved SÃ¡nchez's inner circle and family.
People should distinguish between real and "fictitious" corruption allegations, says el momento mÃ¡s trascendental.
His former transport minister JosÃ© Luis Ãbalos has been given 24 years in prison over multiple corruption offences.
Leading party figure Santos CerdÃ¡n awaits trial for alleged bribery and denies wrongdoing.
SÃ¡nchez's wife BegoÃ±a GÃ³mez faces trial for alleged misuse of public funds and using her marriage to further her academic career. She denies wrongdoing. And his brother David SÃ¡nchez has been banned from public office for nine years for administrative misconduct.
FeijÃ³o has made clear his objective is to form a majority and make "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox. As far as a coalition is concerned, he says he will respect the will of Spanish voters, but maintains Abascal has never talked to him about running any ministries.
The PP leader is clear that Vox's national priority policy would run counter to Spain's constitution and European Union treaties: "No-one can sign illegal agreements."
Even if they were to go into coalition, Camino Mortera-Martinez of the Centre for European Reform, and a former European affairs adviser to the Spanish prime minister is not convinced Vox would wield much influence.
"They're not going to get any of the core ministries. They're not going to get defence or home affairs or foreign policy or economy," she told the BBC. Even if they take over the education ministry, Mortera-Martinez argues education policy is largely devolved to Spain's regional governments.
The leader of Vox, Santiago Abascal, is hoping to double his party's seats in parliament
Since 2022, Vox has worked with the PP in a series of regional coalition governments, holding ministries such as culture and tourism. At the time FeijÃ³o had reservations about Vox joining the conservatives in government in Castilla y LeÃ³n.
The following year they went into coalition with the conservatives in Valencia, AragÃ³n, Murcia, and Extremadura, but pulled out of all five governments in 2024 when they refused to accept unaccompanied migrant children being moved to their regions.
They have since signed new coalition pacts with the PP in Extremadura, AragÃ³n, Castilla y LeÃ³n and Andalusia.
Unlike many European countries Spain has 17 autonomous communities (and two cities) that have their own parliament and their own powers. Catalonia in the north-east and the Basque Country in the north have their own police forces.
The regions matter to Sunday's result. Catalonia alone has 48 seats out of the 350 in Spain's parliament, and the Socialists have recently come to rely on regional parties for support.
SÃ¡nchez's government relied on the support of Basque separatists Bildu and two Catalan parties, ERC on the left and Junts on the right. But when Junts refused to back his housing reform, he decided to dissolve parliament.
Spain is made up of 50 constituencies which each have a minimum of two seats.
The exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla both have one, and the other 248 seats are divided proportionally according to voter numbers.
Madrid province will have 38 seats, Barcelona 32 and Valencia 16.

articles.title_orig: The Other Nvidia Romance With an Executive at a Company Linked to China
articles.title_zh: The Other Nvidia Romance With an Executive at a Company Linked to China
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
A little-known figure in the palace intrigue involving Nvidia's Jensen Huang and possible chip smuggling is rapidly gaining attention. Ying Cenly Chen, a former senior executive at Super Micro Computer , is alleged to have managed a significant portion of the company's purchases of Nvidia chips during the period when Supermicro's hardware was allegedly diverted to China, according to a lawsuit. Her new company, ChronoScale, where Chen serves as CEO, has business ties to both Supermicro and Nvidia.
Chen matters because of her position at Supermicro and because of when she left. A shareholder lawsuit claims that Chen, 50, controlled Supermicro's supply of Nvidia chips and could not have been unaware of the company's alleged illicit sales. She exited Supermicro within weeks of an indictment that named Supermicro co-founder, Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw in the smuggling scheme. She is also married to Ajay "Jay" Puri, Nvidia's longtime sales chief, Chen confirmed to Fortune . Puri worked for the chipmaker for two decades before announcing his retirement in June.
That means Chen could hold some answers to the question now looming large above Nvidia, which is whether Huang, who resigned as CEO on Nov. 11, knew or turned a blind eye as its chips were potentially diverted to China. And it puts a spotlight on her role at ChronoScale, which develops datacenters that rely heavily on Nvidia chips.
Chen disputes the lawsuit's account. In emails to Fortune , she said controlling customer allocations of Nvidia chips "was not part of my job responsibility" when she worked at Supermicro. Supermicro also denied that she controlled how its supply of Nvidia GPUs were distributed.
Chen also said she agreed to join ChronoScale before the Supermicro smuggling scandal broke. She told Fortune she accepted the offer on March 10 via DocuSign , nine days before the Liaw indictment was unsealed on March 19. She said the "offer documentation was completed on April 24" and her last day at Supermicro was April 30. That timing would mean Chen remained as chief growth officer at Supermicro for seven weeks after she said she accepted the ChronoScale job, and for six weeks after the indictment.
Liaw, the Supermicro cofounder, was arrested and indicted with two others in a sweeping $2.5 billion smuggling case in March. Liaw has pleaded not guilty; one of his codefendants, Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun, has pleaded guilty. On a May 5 earnings call , days after Chen's departure, Supermicro CEO Charles Liang told analysts that "no one" at the company other than the three who had been indicted were involved in the alleged scheme. That declaration, which stunned some observers, came while the Supermicro board was still engaged in an ongoing investigation directors launched following Liaw's arrest. Under typical circumstances, Liang as CEO and co-founder who knew Liaw for three decades, wouldn't have been closely involved in an independent board-led investigation, particularly one that was ongoing at the time.
Neither Liang nor Supermicro have been named as targets in the alleged scheme, and Supermicro has said it is itself a victim and is cooperating with authorities. ChronoScale has also not been named by regulators as the target of any investigation. Puri and Nvidia declined to comment. A Supermicro spokesperson denied that Chen controlled how Nvidia GPUs were distributed to customers and said that after 18 years at Supermicro, Chen "voluntarily resigned in early 2026 to take the CEO role at ChronoScale."
It wasn't until August that the Supermicro board's investigation officially concluded with a finding that the investigation team "did not find any evidence that any current member of senior management had knowledge" about the alleged scheme. By that time, Chen had landed as CEO of ChronoScale, an AI cloud company based in Silicon Valley formed on May 5, 2026, when data-center developer Applied Digital merged its GPU cloud subsidiary, Applied Digital Cloud, into Ekso Bionics Holdings, a Nasdaq-listed maker of robotic exoskeletons. The combined company renamed itself ChronoScale and Applied Digital owns about 96% of it.
Now, a shareholder complaint filed in October has cast a cloud over Chen herself. In a complaint filed Oct. 9 in federal court in San Francisco, former Supermicro employees who are not named allege that Chen controlled Supermicro's supply of Nvidia chips and that she left because of the U.S. government's smuggling investigation. Chen is not a defendant in the lawsuit, she has not been charged or accused of wrongdoing by any government agency, and the allegations are unproven.
The lawsuit is a securities class action brought by investors who say Supermicro, Liang and other executives misled them about company sales and export compliance while servers were being allegedly diverted illegally to China, and that they lost money when the March indictment by federal prosecutors in Manhattan sent the stock tanking.
Chen worked at Supermicro from March 2008 to April 2026 and was most recently its chief growth officer and a senior vice president, according to ChronoScale's filings. According to Chronoscale's website, she graduated with a Bachelor's Degree in Science from Fudan University, a public university in Shanghai. The shareholder complaint describes her as a force inside Supermicro who "reported directly to" Liang and led a sales team that it says accounted for "approximately 80% of the company's total sales."
One former employee quoted in the lawsuit, described as a Supermicro sales director from July 2023 to July 2025, said Chen "had a very close relationship with Nvidia and managed the company's acquisition of GPU chips from Nvidia." Because the supply was limited and in such demand, the former employee said Nvidia "would allocate a certain number to Super Micro, and Chen decided how to distribute them among Super Micro's customers." Chen met routinely with Liang "to obtain Liang's approval of how the chips would be allocated," according to the complaint.
Supermicro disputes this allegation. "Cenly Chen did not control how Nvidia GPUs were distributed to customers," the spokesperson said.
A second former employee in the lawsuit, described as a sales director who worked at Supermicro until 2024, said Chen "handled all allocations of Nvidia chips to Super Micro" and had taken over responsibility for the sales team that covered China. The person said "there was no way Cenly Chen lacked knowledge of the company's illicit sales."
The complaint also offers an account of why Chen left. The first former employee claimed that Chen's emails had created a potentially problematic paper trail: "It was widely known within the company that Chen had to leave because she had sent emails requesting that Nvidia release chips with serial numbers associated with the GPUs illegally diverted to customers in China." Citing the former employee, the complaint also states she "resigned so that the company could claim that no current employees were involved in the scheme for which Liaw was arrested."
Chen disputes the account.
"I do not believe this email exists, as I would never knowingly do such a thing and I don't believe I ever did," Chen told Fortune . Both former employees had left Supermicro before Chen did, according to the complaint's own description of their tenures, and it does not say how they learned the circumstances of her departure.
ChronoScale was created on May 5, when Applied Digital's cloud business merged into Ekso Bionics Holdings, a public company. Chen's hiring was not disclosed in securities filings before then. The offer letter ChronoScale filed with the SEC is dated May 5 and shows Chen's acceptance dated April 24.
On April 3, more than three weeks after Chen says she accepted the job, Ekso mailed its shareholders an information statement describing the planned merger. It listed "the directors and executive officers of ChronoScale following the Business Combinati

articles.title_orig: Stocks rally in Asia, US tariffs not as dire as feared
articles.title_zh: Stocks rally in Asia, US tariffs not as dire as feared
articles.content_orig:
Global stocks rallied on Thursday, staging a tentative recovery from an intense AI-driven sell-off and looked past a fresh set of tariffs unveiled by the White House on Wednesday.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and will have a shortened trading session on Friday. During Wednesday's regular session, the Dow gained 0.33%, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 0.62% and the S&P 500 shed 0.25%.
In Europe on Thursday, equities rose sharply. The pan-European Stoxx 600 was 1.4% higher shortly after the opening bell, with all sectors and major bourses in positive territory.
Germany's DAX led gains on a rise of 1.7%, while the Stoxx 600 Technology index jumped almost 2%. The regional tech index has lost more than 12% so far this month, amid jitters around a potential AI bubble bursting and the ousting — and return — of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO.
German semiconductor firm Infineon was more than 4% higher in early trading, as chip stocks notched a boost. ASMI and ASML gained 2.8% and 2.4%, respectively, while Be Semiconductor added close to 3%.
Asia-Pacific markets also rose on Thursday.
South Korea's Kospi gained 0.29% to close at 4,711.21, while the small-cap Kosdaq index advanced 0.78% to 655.71 after the country's central bank hiked benchmark lending rates to a 2-year high, in its final meeting of the year.
Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.86% to 57,499.16 while the Topix edged 0.11% higher to 3,750.4. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.82% to 8,763.8.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was up 1.52% in its last hour of trade, while mainland China's CSI 300 edged higher marginally, closing at 3,900.55.
Asian technology stocks rebounded sharply Thursday, led by Japanese chip-related companies.
SoftBank Group surged more than 7%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest rose 4.57%. Lasertec and Disco gained , while Tokyo Electron climbed 0.59%
In South Korea, memory chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics advanced more than 2% and 0.35%, respectively. The gains followed a bruising session Wednesday amid renewed concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence spending.
Cryptocurrencies also traded higher, with bitcoin rising 1.58% to $60,944.60, while ether gained 1.15% to $1,702.96.
The gains come amid lingering concerns over the outlook for digital assets, with the co-founder of now-shuttered crypto exchange BitMEX Arthur Hayes telling CNBC on Tuesday that bitcoin could test $50,000 if the Nasdaq continues to slide.
Meanwhile, fresh U.S. inflation data reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year on year in October, accelerating from 3.7% in September, while core inflation came in slightly above expectations at 3.3%.

articles.title_orig: S. Korea's spy agency denies report about China's alleged proposal for anti-US operations
articles.title_zh: S. Korea's spy agency denies report about China's alleged proposal for anti-US operations
articles.content_orig:
Published : Nov. 26, 2026 - 10:24:22
Add The Korea Herald on Google
South Korea's spy agency has denied a media report that Beijing had proposed covert operations against the United States when the agency sought to secure the release of two informants detained by China early this year.
The Kukmin Daily reported Wednesday that China made the proposal to the National Intelligence Service for the anti-US operations, and that Washington strongly protested it, apparently leading to a chasm in the South Korea-US intelligence partnership.
"The NIS has never received any such proposal from the Chinese authorities," it said in a press notice.
The agency also said intelligence cooperation between Seoul and Washington is proceeding in a "two-way" and "mutually beneficial" manner across various fields, including counterintelligence.
Concerns about bilateral intelligence collaboration have continued following reports earlier this year that the US partially limited Seoul's access to its satellite-based intelligence on North Korea after Unification Minister Chung Dong-young referred to the North's Kusong area as one of the uranium enrichment sites.
Seoul believes that Chung's reference to the Kusong site is based on "open-source" information, while the US side regards it as a disclosure of confidential US information.
Commenting on intelligence cooperation between Seoul and Washington, a senior US official told Yonhap News Agency last month that the US expects South Korea to "uphold the standards of our decadeslong alliance, in particular concerning matters of intelligence and counterintelligence."
Meanwhile, a South Korean engineer, who previously worked for a Korean firm, has been detained in China for nearly three years following his arrest on espionage charges in December 2023, according to a government source. The person has been suspected of informing the NIS of suspected leaks of South Korean semiconductor technology.
The NIS is believed to have started earnest efforts for the detainee's release after President Lee Jae Myung's administration took office last year.
The agency is said to have even considered negotiating a "swap deal" in the first half of this year, offering information on an illegal intelligence agent, known as a "black" operative, in exchange for its citizen's release. The black operative was reportedly affiliated with a third country, not the US or Japan. (Yonhap)

articles.title_orig: Billions in Data Center Deals Grind to Halt After AI Chip Curbs
articles.title_zh: Billions in Data Center Deals Grind to Halt After AI Chip Curbs
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.
Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.
Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.
The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.
The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.
Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people.
Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.
The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.
In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI , of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes."
"For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he said.
"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries."
During Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.

articles.title_orig: Norse Atlantic flights suspended after warning finances 'critical'
articles.title_zh: Norse Atlantic flights suspended after warning finances 'critical'
articles.content_orig:
Norse Atlantic suspended all of its flights on Thursday and warned it may have to file for bankruptcy after its stock collapsed on Wednesday following its warning about its "critical" financial situation.
Oslo-listed shares of Norse closed 85% lower on Wednesday.
"The board of directors continues to consider options to secure short-term financing," Norse said in a Thursday statement. "If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the board's intention to file for bankruptcy."
The airline added that "there can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found."
Checks by CNBC showed the airline was still selling tickets for flights on Friday and beyond as of 9 a.m. Oslo time on Thursday.
Warning signs first popped up when PK786 from London to Islamabad and PK710 from Manchester to Lahore were cancelled because of "an unexpected operational suspension," the Pakistani flag carrier said on X.
The airline had been set to operate two Pakistan International Airlines flights Wednesday under a wet-lease agreement, in which one airline provides the aircraft and crew to another. The agreement had only been signed in early October.
PIA said it would operate the routes using its own Boeing 777 aircraft from the next day.
Norse's own flight Z0 783 from London Gatwick to Orlando was also shown as canceled Wednesday on live air traffic website Flightradar24. London Gatwick's website listed the flight's status for Thursday as "enquire airline."
In a bid to stave off financial troubles, Norse cut 75 jobs in May as part of an effort to reduce costs by $50 million, after Eivind Roald replaced founder Bjorn Tore Larsen as CEO in November last year.
The Norwegian carrier said Wednesday that its situation depended on securing financing for short-term liquidity needs and that it was in discussions about a potential strategic takeover.
"Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution," the airline said.
The Norwegian carrier has come under strain due to soaring jet fuel costs since the onset of the Iran war.
India's largest airline, low-cost carrier IndiGo, entered an agreement with Norse Atlantic in early 2025 to lease six 787-9 aircraft as it launched flights to Europe and Britain ahead of the arrival of its own widebody planes.
The agreement concluded at the end of October this year, with IndiGo citing airspace constraints, elevated fuel costs and currency pressures.
At its peak in 2024, Norse Atlantic had 4,822 scheduled flights. That number dipped to 4,695 in 2025 and 2,565 in 2026, according to aviation analytics company Cirium. The airline had 122 flights scheduled for November this year.
Norse Atlantic CEO Roald told CNBC in May that he was not "overly concerned" about access to fuel and said the airline had no indication at the time that the crisis would have an immediate impact. The airline said in October that it was continuing to operate at reduced capacity because of "prolonged high fuel prices."
Correction: This story was updated to reflect that Norse shares closed 85% lower on Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: Xi unleashes China ‘earthquake’ with shock ouster of rising star
articles.title_zh: Xi unleashes China ‘earthquake’ with shock ouster of rising star
articles.content_orig:
He was on the rise among China’s political elite, hosting tech leaders and senior American officials. But now Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s influential politburo, appears to be the latest senior official brought down by President Xi Jinping’s sweeping purge.
The hammer unexpectedly came down on Chen in the form of a two-line bulletin on the Xinhua news agency Tuesday: He is “suspected of serious violations of Party discipline and law and is currently under disciplinary review and supervisory investigation” — a common euphemism for corruption crackdowns on ruling Communist Party officials under Xi.
Public announcements such as these usually mark the end of a political career in China. Chen has made no public statement.
He is the fourth politburo member to be purged in less than two years, part of a broader crackdown that has swept aside top military leaders as Xi consolidates power. He is set to extend his rule next year, at a party congress that is held once every five years and looms over the preceding months.
But Chen’s abrupt downfall took many close observers of China by surprise, given his profile and career path would usually point to a bright future.
“He was potentially going to the highest level, which would be the standing committee. And I think from a lot of Western observers, people thought he had even better prospects,” Damien Ma, the Singapore-based director of the Carnegie China think tank, told NBC News.
Some analysts have speculated that Xi, increasingly viewed as likely to rule for life, may have been purging a viable replacement. Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London, said however that Chen was “someone who could rise further but not as a successor.”
Chen, a 62-year-old technocrat known as a friend of foreign business and an advocate for AI, was an environmental scientist who studied in London and swiftly rose through the party’s ranks. He served as China’s environmental minister, Beijing’s mayor and the party secretary in Shanghai — a post once held by Xi and widely considered a stepping stone to bigger things.
Just last month, Chen hosted Apple Chairman Tim Cook, welcoming the U.S. tech giant to “make full use of Shanghai’s strengths” and bring more products to the city, a financial and cultural hub that has long served as a connection between China and the international community.
In his last public appearance last week, during a tour of a shipping facility, Chen called for advancing the industry’s digital transformation.
By Wednesday, Chen’s name has been removed from some official websites. A webpage on the Shanghai government site showing that meeting with Cook is now showing a 404 message, or not found.
Chen is just the latest senior official in the crosshairs of Xi’s long-running anti-corruption campaign and emphasis on party discipline, which analysts say is as much about loyalty as it is about reform.
“It is a warning to all technocrats, as Chen was a rising star among technocrats and had no apparent failures in a technocratic way. So, message is: adhere to strict party discipline and demonstrate unquestionable loyalty to Xi or else,” Tsang said.
The party’s Central Committee, which has about 200 mostly male leaders, vowed to “ensure more rigorous discipline enforcement, and make full use of discipline as a guide, restraint, guarantee, and incentive” at its closed-door gathering, the fifth plenum, last month.
“What they’ve been building as part of this discipline machine over the last 15 years is to kind of implement their sort of internal operating system of how they deal with, let’s say, bad eggs within the party,” Ma, of Carnegie China, said.
“The top leadership is normalizing this anti-corruption, this self-cleansing,” Ma said. “It is now a normal part of what the party expects, and they’re trying to embed that over time and down to every single level,” he added.
The Chinese government has not announced any charges against Chen, who was the youngest member of the country’s elite decision-making body. The 24-member Politburo was unveiled in 2022 but is now down to 21 members after the purges. Last month, top general Zhang Shengmin was elevated to the body in a rare addition.
Chen’s undoing comes a year before the party’s top leadership is reshuffled at the 21st Communist Party Congress, when Xi is expected to solidify control even further and cement another five-year term at the helm of the country.
Born in 1964, Chen studied at the prestigious Tsinghua university, long a major pipeline for senior party officials and where he served as president from 2012 to 2015. His name has now been removed from Tsinghua’s online list of former presidents.
After studying at Tsinghua in the 1980s, he moved for a decade to Britain, where he obtained a doctorate from Imperial College London in 1993.
Chen returned to Tsinghua’s environmental science and engineering department in 1998 before being named the university’s president in 2012, according to an official biography .
He’s authored dozens of papers, including on carbon emission reduction and water quality monitoring .
The relatively young Chen would ride around campus on his bike and built a reputation for pushing institutional reforms in his three years at the helm of the university, according to an article in People’s Digest , a magazine affiliated with the People’s Daily, the community party’s official newspaper.
The article, titled “From University President to Cabinet Minister,” was published in 2015, the same year he was picked to lead the Environmental Protection Ministry. In 2017, Chen became mayor of the capital, Beijing, where he oversaw the 2022 Winter Olympics during the Covid pandemic.
Later that year he was transferred to Shanghai and became the party chief, a coveted role that Xi took on himself in 2007 before becoming the country’s leader in 2013.
There, he became heavily involved with the tech industry, regularly hosting CEOs and advocating for more investment into Shanghai, where the World AI Conference was hosted earlier this year.
Chen hosted Elon Musk in 2023 to discuss Tesla’s operations in the city. Last year, he accompanied Xi to an AI hub there. And last month, Chen met with several European tech leaders, in addition to hosting Cook.
Alongside the top post in Shanghai, Chen also was elected for a five-year term as a member of the Politburo, China’s elite decision-making body headed by Xi.
While the Politburo is not the absolute apex of power, he was seen as a contender the much-smaller Politburo’s Standing Committee, which is made up of the country’s highest ranking officials.
“If you’re party secretary of one of the four big municipalities, Beijing, Shanghai, Chongqing and Tianjin, you have pretty good prospects. That’s sort of an indication that you’re on your way up,” Ma said.
Whether or not Chen’s ousting deals a blow to the country’s technology ambitions and its race for dominance in artificial intelligence, remains to be seen, Ma said. But either way, his downfall will force a rethink among those seeking to predict the route to power in modern China.
“Part of it is thinking through what is really the new criteria to get to the top, and they may not be what we thought just a few months ago,” Ma added.
Max Burman is deputy editor in the London bureau of NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Spanish elections: What you need to know and what's at stake
articles.title_zh: Spanish elections: What you need to know and what's at stake
articles.content_orig:
After eight years of Socialist-led government under Pedro Sánchez, Spain is at a crossroads.
Snap elections are taking place on Sunday 29 November, and voters face a choice of continued left-wing rule or a conservative-led government, with the likely support of far-right Vox.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo's conservative People's Party is narrowly ahead of the Socialist PSOE in most polls.
He has spoken of Spain being probably at "the most significant moment in our country for the past 50 years", and he aims to "repair the state, regenerate democracy, reunited the nation and recover Spain's ambition and self-esteem". But it is unlikely he could do anything without the backing of Vox, who are third in the opinion polls.
For more on Feijóo and who else to watch in this election - read here .
Spain has a population of almost 50 million, and almost 39 million people have the right to vote for the Congress and the upper house, the Senate. The polls open at 09:00 (08:00 GMT) on Sunday and close at 20:00 (19:00 GMT), when the first exit polls come out.
Sánchez called this vote eight months early after MPs rejected planned changes to Spain's housing laws.
He was responding to nationwide protests after an 87-year-old woman called Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her rented flat in Madrid and later died.
But his government lost the support of a centre-right party called Junts from the north-eastern region of Catalonia which sought to protect the rights of property owners.
Housing remains one of the hot-button issues for voters, but they are also focused on the high cost of living, corruption and immigration. And the election takes place within weeks of a devastating rail disaster that has shattered confidence in Spain’s high-speed rail network.
Spain's property prices and rents have soared by more than 80% from 2015 to 2025, and wages have not kept pace.
Spain has a combination of high demand and scarce supply: the Bank of Spain estimates 700,000 homes are needed to ease the pressure.
The result is that millions of Spaniards have little chance to buy a house, while they live in fear of eviction if their rent is increased. On 11 November, four million Spaniards were galvanised into joining the first general strike since 2012, according to the unions.
Pedro Sánchez has embraced housing reform as a big campaign issue and left-wing parties have promised rent controls and protection against eviction, while the right is focusing on building more homes, tax breaks for homebuyers and planning deregulation.
Support for the Socialists is down from 2023, but even then he came second in the race and relied on the backing of other parties, mainly on the left, to stay in power. This time those other left-wing parties, in particular the Broad Front (Frente Amplio) have fallen back and the big questions now are more about Feijóo's conservatives.
"It is a demobilisation of the left. Sanchez's party is not doing well," says Jacobo Ramos Folch, Policy Analyst and visiting professor at the University of Navarra.
"That lack of majority is really a reality – and the rise of Vox. What is changing that shift of majorities is the rise of Vox."
Vox have been around since 2013 but polls suggest this time they could almost double their 33 seats in Spain's lower house, the Congress.
Their big themes are "national priority" – putting Spanish citizens first for subsidies and welfare, along with repatriating migrants "in an illegal situation" and "remigration" of foreigners who do not contribute to Spain.
Migration has become a key challenge for Spain, and Alberto Nuñez Feijoo has accused his rival of being a "problem for Europe when it comes to immigration" after the influx of tens of thousands of migrants into the exclave of Ceuta from neighbouring Morocco in July.
This month too, the Canary Island of El Hierro has seen record arrivals, with 2,000 people landing there on 24 November. Abascal has spoken of "another invasion".
And yet a recent CIS survey put it far behind housing, cost of living, healthcare and working conditions.
The PP and Vox have bitterly criticised the Socialist-led government for a drive to legalise unauthorised migrants this year that attracted 1.2 million applications.
Feijóo's party wants to see more controlled immigration. Vox has called for mass deportations.
Feijóo has accused the Socialists of being "the most corrupt party" that Spain has ever seen, and a number of cases have involved Sánchez's inner circle and family.
People should distinguish between real and "fictitious" corruption allegations, says el momento más trascendental.
His former transport minister José Luis Ábalos has been given 24 years in prison over multiple corruption offences.
Leading party figure Santos Cerdán awaits trial for alleged bribery and denies wrongdoing.
Sánchez's wife Begoña Gómez faces trial for alleged misuse of public funds and using her marriage to further her academic career. She denies wrongdoing. And his brother David Sánchez has been banned from public office for nine years for administrative misconduct.
Feijóo has made clear his objective is to form a majority and make "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox. As far as a coalition is concerned, he says he will respect the will of Spanish voters, but maintains Abascal has never talked to him about running any ministries.
The PP leader is clear that Vox's national priority policy would run counter to Spain's constitution and European Union treaties: "No-one can sign illegal agreements."
Even if they were to go into coalition, Camino Mortera-Martinez of the Centre for European Reform, and a former European affairs adviser to the Spanish prime minister is not convinced Vox would wield much influence.
"They're not going to get any of the core ministries. They're not going to get defence or home affairs or foreign policy or economy," she told the BBC. Even if they take over the education ministry, Mortera-Martinez argues education policy is largely devolved to Spain's regional governments.
Since 2022, Vox has worked with the PP in a series of regional coalition governments, holding ministries such as culture and tourism. At the time Feijóo had reservations about Vox joining the conservatives in government in Castilla y León.
The following year they went into coalition with the conservatives in Valencia, Aragón, Murcia, and Extremadura, but pulled out of all five governments in 2024 when they refused to accept unaccompanied migrant children being moved to their regions.
They have since signed new coalition pacts with the PP in Extremadura, Aragón, Castilla y León and Andalusia.
Unlike many European countries Spain has 17 autonomous communities (and two cities) that have their own parliament and their own powers. Catalonia in the north-east and the Basque Country in the north have their own police forces.
The regions matter to Sunday's result. Catalonia alone has 48 seats out of the 350 in Spain's parliament, and the Socialists have recently come to rely on regional parties for support.
Sánchez's government relied on the support of Basque separatists Bildu and two Catalan parties, ERC on the left and Junts on the right. But when Junts refused to back his housing reform, he decided to dissolve parliament.
Spain is made up of 50 constituencies which each have a minimum of two seats.
The exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla both have one, and the other 248 seats are divided proportionally according to voter numbers.
Madrid province will have 38 seats, Barcelona 32 and Valencia 16.
To win a seat, a party has to win 3% of the vote in a province, but in smaller provinces with fewer seats parties generally need more than that.

SpaceX said on Wednesday it would contribute one newly issued Class A share to every currently active Trump Account, the tax-advantaged investment accounts created for American children.
CEO Elon Musk will personally match the number of shares the company donates, consistent with his earlier pledge to give one SpaceX share to every kid in America. President and COO Gwynne Shotwell separately announced a personal gift of more than 2 million shares.

It is the first U.S. authorization of its kind. The solar-powered modules would process data in space for use on Earth, using optical links supplemented by radiofrequency communications.
Chairman Brendan Carr described the decision as opening a new frontier for computing infrastructure to support U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence. Musk called the approval "a great asset to America and the world."
SpaceX has until late 2033 for its first operational satellite, until 2035 for 100,000 satellites, and until 2040 for the full constellation.

While RKLB closed up 2% after opening down 5%, ASTS ended the day 10% higher after briefly touching a fresh 52-week low. LUNR, meanwhile, closed up 2%, after falling as much as 10% intraday.
Rocket Lab is now targeting no earlier than 27 November 2026 for its next Electron launch, a mission named "Night Owls Never Sleep" that will deploy Synspective's 14th StriX synthetic-aperture radar satellite. The flight will be Rocket Lab's 101st Electron launch overall and its 14th for the Japanese Earth-observation company. Rocket Lab remains Synspective's sole launch provider and has another 33 Electron missions under contract with the customer through 2031, even as the company develops its Neutron launch vehicle.
Meanwhile, airspace coordination materials from Caribbean and South American air traffic management this week list a tentative 20 February 2027 date for Blue Origin's New Glenn 5 flight, which AST SpaceMobile's prior commentary have associated with its satellites BlueBirds 17, 18 and19. Blue Origin has yet to confirm the launch date. Previously, the three satellites launch was slated for the first quarter of 2027, without a specific launch date.

articles.title_orig: South Korea's Kospi leads gains as tech rebound lifts Asia markets
articles.title_zh: South Korea's Kospi leads gains as tech rebound lifts Asia markets
articles.content_orig:
Asia-Pacific markets rose Thursday, tracking Wall Street gains overnight, with tech stocks rebounding from steep losses in the prior session.
South Korea's Kospi gained 1.73%, while the small-cap Kosdaq index advanced 2.32% after the country's central bank hiked benchmark lending rates by an expected 25 basis points, as inflation continues to run above target while a booming economy allows it room to tighten policy.
The central bank raised rates to 3.25%, a 2-year high, in its final meeting of the year, data on the Bank of Korea's website showed .
Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 1.21% in early trade, while the Topix edged 0.71% higher. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.15%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index rose 1.46% while mainland China's CSI 300 added 0.12%.
Asian technology stocks rebounded sharply Thursday, led by Japanese chip-related companies.
SoftBank Group surged more than 11%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest rose 7.3%. Lasertec and Disco both gained more than 6%, while Tokyo Electron climbed 4.6%.
In South Korea, memory chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics advanced more than 4% and 2.1%, respectively. The gains followed a bruising session Wednesday amid renewed concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence spending.
Investors appears to have looked past a fresh set of U.S. tariffs unveiled by the White House on Wednesday, targeting more than a dozen major trading partners, including China and the European Union.
Meanwhile, fresh U.S. inflation data reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year on year in October, accelerating from 3.7% in September, while core inflation came in slightly above expectations at 3.3%.
Overnight in the U.S., the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased an 1,100-point plunge on Wednesday, advancing 164.25 points, or 0.33%, to end at 50,182.95. The Nasdaq Composite , however, fell 0.62% to 23,585.80, while the S&P 500 shed 0.25% to close at 7,182.78.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and will have a shortened trading session on Friday.

articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Billionaire Boehly signs US-backed share swap deal to buy Lukoil global assets
articles.content_orig:
Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly's asset management company Eldridge have struck a deal to buy Lukoil's assets outside of Russia, sources confirmed to CNBC.
The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and Catena Investments, based in the United Arab Emirates, are also parties to the deal, the sources said.
The deal transfers Lukoil's international refineries and other production assets in Bulgaria, Romania, Africa and the Middle East to the U.S.-led group, the sources said. It also includes retail gas stations in the U.S., Europe and Asia, they said.
The U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control is expected to sign off on the deal but final approval is still needed, the sources said. The deal would give the U.S.-led group about 350,000 barrels per day of production.
The agreement would allow Europe to buy fuel such as diesel previously produced by Lukoil through the U.S.-led group rather than Russia.

articles.title_zh: Trump unveils new tariffs over excess industrial capacity, undeterred by midterms defeat
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Sabrina Valle and Tom Wilson
NEW YORK/LONDON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Global markets retreated on Wednesday with riskier assets under pressure after the Trump administration proposed sweeping new tariffs on 14 trading partners.
US stocks, hammered in the morning, partially recovered in the afternoon ‌from early losses as investors bought the dip ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. The Dow closed higher and the Nasdaq and S&P ‌500 ended slightly lower.
US technology shares led declines amid concerns about inflation and a hawkish Federal Reserve, while investors assessed the implications of the tariffs for global supply chains and economic ​growth. Treasury prices rose as investors sought safe-haven assets.
MSCI's global stocks index fell 0.60% and Nvidia shed more than 8% during the day before closing down 3.91%.
Oliver Pursche, senior vice president at Wealthspire Advisors, said bargain hunters were stepping in ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, adding that "investors are taking advantage of some of those discrepancies."
The Nasdaq was down more than 4% earlier in the session before closing down 0.62%, with the S&P 500 falling 0.25% and the Dow up 0.33%.
The ‌selloff was mirrored elsewhere, with Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan ⁠down 1.99% and emerging market stocks falling 2.8%.
"We still have not dealt with the fresh shock of Nvidia and tech and now we have tariffs," said Aneeka Gupta, an equity strategist at WisdomTree.
"Markets are contending with AI, central banks ⁠remain hawkish, and then if we get a renewal of tariffs that adds volatility in markets."
European shares, which had traded higher earlier on gains in personal and household goods and retail stocks, later reversed course. The pan-European STOXX 600 fell 1.06%.
Earlier in the day, the broad selloff, combined with lower bond yields, signaled growing concern that ​escalating ​trade barriers could weigh on global growth and corporate earnings. By the close of ​the US stock market, copper and aluminum prices had risen, ‌and bitcoin had gained 0.81%.
US Treasury yields declined on Wednesday but were off their earlier lows. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note fell 6.2 basis points to 4.84% and was on pace for its seventh daily drop in the past eight sessions.
Nvidia gave up part of its gains from earlier this week, leaving the stock down about 10% since Monday, when CEO Jensen Huang's return sparked a 31.5% rally. S&P Global Ratings put the company at risk of a rating downgrade.
Data showed US consumer confidence increased by more than expected in November to its highest level in nearly ‌two years. Separately, data showed the US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the ​third quarter, and inflation increased further in October.
The dollar index, which measures the US ​currency against a basket of major peers including the yen and ​euro, fell 0.14%, while the euro was up 0.11% to $1.09.
The inflation and growth data reinforced expectations that the Federal ‌Reserve will raise interest rates next month and again in ​early 2027.
Euro zone government bond yields fell ​as the slide in US equities drove investors towards the relative safety of sovereign debt. Germany's benchmark 10-year Bund yield fell 4.73 basis points to 3.218%, from 3.266% late on Tuesday.
Brent crude futures LCOc1 settled $3.21, or 3.5%, higher at $94.61 a barrel, after Yemen's Houthis said they ​had attacked Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery. [O/R]
Trading volume was ‌low, and US markets will be closed Thursday.
(Reporting by Sabrina Valle and Caroline Valetkevitch in New York and Tom Wilson in ​London; additional reporting by Chuck Mikolajczak in New York, Dhara Ranasinghe in London, Gregor Stuart Hunter in Singapore and Roger Tung ​in Taipei. Editing by DJ Yap, Gareth Jones, Mark Potter and Deepa Babington)

articles.title_orig: S&P warns Nvidia's board may be compromised, puts chipmaker's rating on downgrade watch
articles.title_zh: S&P warns Nvidia's board may be compromised, puts chipmaker's rating on downgrade watch
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's credit rating could be cut by one notch over the next 90 days if the company continues to have "deficiencies" in its management and governance framework, S&P Global Ratings said in the wake of the Jensen Huang's ouster and reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.
"News regarding the CEO and questions regarding potential export control violations have exposed vulnerabilities in Nvidia's management and governance framework, especially in regard to its board structure, composition, and effectiveness," S&P said in a Wednesday note .
Nvidia currently holds an AA rating, the third-highest level.
S&P has placed the chipmaker on "CreditWatch with negative implications," though any potential downgrade would be limited to one notch, to AA-, unless investigations or disclosures lead the agency to conclude that Nvidia's reputation or future prospects have also been harmed.
A downgrade can pressure bond prices, push yields higher and raise borrowing costs. Nvidia priced $25 billion of investment-grade senior notes in June, with maturities from 2028 through 2056, shortly after S&P upgraded the company from AA- to AA.
Nvidia has about $32.5 billion of bonds in the U.S. high-grade corporate bond index, according to Bloomberg.
S&P's Wednesday note follows Moody's Ratings changing its outlook on Nvidia to stable from positive on Nov. 18, citing governance concerns, and leaving that outlook unchanged after Huang's return on Monday.
In its note, S&P cited the "long tenure" of certain board members as a reason their independence may be "compromised" and said Nvidia's management and governance risk was "rising."
The ratings agency added that it remained unaware of any remedial action taken by the board to address what could be "meaningful" management and governance deficiencies.
Chairman Harvey Jones and early investor Tench Coxe have served on Nvidia's board since 1993, while Brooke Seawell joined in 1997. Mark Stevens served from 1993 to 2006 and rejoined the board in 2008.
S&P also flagged questions around geopolitical risk management and internal controls arising from Nvidia's exposure to China.
"While Nvidia management has delivered significant returns for its stakeholders over decades, weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning have brought questions around the "key man" risk to the forefront," S&P's Andrew Chang and David Tsui said.
Chang and Tsui noted that Huang's resignation and subsequent reinstatement did not resolve questions about the board's oversight of executive conduct.
The agency also intends to meet with Nvidia's board and management to discuss plans to address those deficiencies, particularly around "board independence, effective management oversight and a credible leadership succession plan."
Huang returned less than two weeks after Jones said Nvidia's directors did not intend to reinstate him. The board later voted unanimously to bring Huang back, sending Nvidia shares up as much as 36% during Monday's session.
Nvidia shares are down about 12.5% since Monday's close.
